{{Short description|On when a set of compact Riemannian manifolds of a given dimension is relatively compact}}
{{distinguish|text = [[Gromov's compactness theorem (topology)|Gromov's compactness theorem in symplectic geometry]]}}
In the [[mathematical]] field of [[metric geometry]], [[Mikhael Gromov (mathematician)|Mikhael Gromov]] proved a fundamental '''compactness theorem''' for sequences of [[metric space]]s. In the special case of [[Riemannian manifolds]], the key assumption of his compactness theorem is automatically satisfied under an assumption on [[Ricci curvature]]. These theorems have been widely used in the fields of [[geometric group theory]] and [[Riemannian geometry]].

==Metric compactness theorem==
The [[Gromov–Hausdorff metric|Gromov–Hausdorff distance]] defines a notion of distance between any two [[metric space]]s, thereby setting up the concept of a sequence of metric spaces which converges to another metric space. This is known as [[Gromov–Hausdorff convergence]]. Gromov found a condition on a sequence of [[compactness (topology)|compact]] metric spaces which ensures that a [[subsequence]] converges to some metric space relative to the Gromov–Hausdorff distance:{{sfnm|1a1=Bridson|1a2=Haefliger|1y=1999|1loc=Theorem 5.41|2a1=Burago|2a2=Burago|2a3=Ivanov|2y=2001|2loc=Theorem 7.4.15|3a1=Gromov|3y=1981|3loc=Section 6|4a1=Gromov|4y=1999|4loc=Proposition 5.2|5a1=Petersen|5y=2016|5loc=Proposition 11.1.10}}
<blockquote>Let {{math|(''X''<sub>''i''</sub>, ''d''<sub>''i''</sub>)}} be a sequence of compact metric spaces with uniformly bounded diameter. Suppose that for every positive number {{math|ε}} there is a [[natural number]] {{mvar|N}} and, for every {{mvar|i}}, the set {{math|''X''<sub>''i''</sub>}} can be covered by {{mvar|N}} [[metric ball]]s of radius {{math|ε}}. Then the sequence {{math|(''X''<sub>''i''</sub>, ''d''<sub>''i''</sub>)}} has a subsequence which converges relative to the Gromov–Hausdorff distance.</blockquote>
The role of this theorem in the theory of Gromov–Hausdorff convergence may be considered as analogous to the role of the [[Arzelà–Ascoli theorem]] in the theory of [[uniform convergence]].{{sfnm|1a1=Villani|1y=2009|1p=754}} Gromov first formally introduced it in his 1981 resolution of the [[Gromov's theorem on groups of polynomial growth|Milnor–Wolf conjecture]] in the field of [[geometric group theory]], where he applied it to define the [[Ultralimit|asymptotic cone]] of certain metric spaces.{{sfnm|1a1=Gromov|1y=1981|1loc=Section 7|2a1=Gromov|2y=1999|2loc=Paragraph 5.7}} These techniques were later extended by Gromov and others, using the theory of [[ultrafilter]]s.{{sfnm|1a1=Bridson|1a2=Haefliger|1y=1999|1loc=Definition 5.50|2a1=Gromov|2y=1993|2loc=Section 2}}

==Riemannian compactness theorem==
Specializing to the setting of [[geodesically complete]] [[Riemannian manifold]]s with a fixed lower bound on the [[Ricci curvature]], the crucial covering condition in Gromov's metric compactness theorem is automatically satisfied as a corollary of the [[Bishop–Gromov inequality|Bishop–Gromov volume comparison theorem]]. As such, it follows that:{{sfnm|1a1=Gromov|1y=1999|1loc=Theorem 5.3|2a1=Petersen|2y=2016|2loc=Corollary 11.1.13}}
<blockquote>Consider a sequence of [[closed manifold|closed]] Riemannian manifolds with a uniform lower bound on the Ricci curvature and a uniform upper bound on the diameter. Then there is a subsequence which converges relative to the Gromov–Hausdorff distance.</blockquote>
The limit of a convergent subsequence may be a metric space without any smooth or Riemannian structure.{{sfnm|1a1=Gromov|1y=1999|1loc=Paragraph 5.5}} This special case of the metric compactness theorem is significant in the field of [[Riemannian geometry]], as it isolates the purely metric consequences of lower Ricci curvature bounds.
